Foreign demand for US Treasury auctions sees biggest drop since 2016 in benchmark 10-year:

A day after Monday’s 3-year Treasury auction tailed (yield above expectations), today's benchmark $42 billion 10-year sale sees biggest tail since February, as indirect bidders (which include foreign buyers) posted their biggest drop since 2016.

▪️ Tail: +1.0 basis point (5.020% high yield vs. 5.010% when-issued), biggest since February, vs. a 1.7 basis point stop-through in October and a 0.6 basis point stop-through six-month average. It ends two straight stop-throughs.

▪️ High yield: 5.020%, lowest since September, vs. 5.300% in October (highest since November 2000) and a 4.734% six-month average. The 5% coupon is the highest since 2006, per ZeroHedge.

▪️ Bid-to-cover: 2.46, lowest since May, vs. 2.77 in October and a 2.60 six-month average.

▪️ Indirect (incl. foreign): 61.2%, lowest since October 2023, vs. 80.3% in October and a 76.7% six-month average. The drop of 19.1 percentage points is the biggest from one auction to the next since July 2016.

▪️ Direct (domestic): 29.0%, highest since September 2013, vs. 17.1% in October and a 15.9% six-month average.

▪️ Dealers: 9.8%, highest since May, vs. 2.5% in October and a 7.4% six-month average.

@investingLive_’s Greg Michalowski graded it a D+: “The auction was a little soft.” ZeroHedge called it “downright ugly,” with foreign buyers staging “a bit of a strike.”

This is now the 5th straight note auction (2-, 5-, 7-, 3- and 10-year) with indirect bidders below their six-month average, and that lack of demand is adding to pressure on yields, although they fell back to just under 5% since the auction (currently 4.988%). Thursday’s $25 billion 30-year is next.

On the readthrough to October core PCE both BofA and Goldman significantly raised their expectations: 

Bank of America said the CPI data “topped our expectations, driven in part by broad-based strength in goods inflation. This could be evidence of energy and AI related input cost pass through.” It is now tracking October core PCE at 0.32% month over month, up from its initial 0.23% estimate, which it said “would lift the y/y rate to 3.3% from 3.1%, which is a clearly hawkish development.” For headline PCE, it is tracking 0.34% and 3.9% from a year earlier.

“Our core PCE tracking estimate would meet Governor Waller’s threshold for a 50bp hike in December based on his remarks from this morning,” Bank of America said. “That helps explain the move in market pricing. We still think the Fed goes 25bp for now, but the door to a larger hike at its next meeting has opened further after today’s data.”

Goldman Sachs now estimates that core PCE rose 0.35% in October, up from its 0.23% expectation before the CPI release, “corresponding to a year-over-year rate of +3.30%,” with headline PCE up 0.36%, or 3.87% from a year earlier.

 It said the core CPI surprise “was driven by firmer-than-expected readings in a broad set of categories,” with owners’ equivalent rent “firm for the second consecutive month” and “concentrated in the Midwest,” and motor vehicle insurance prices rebounding “after running softer this year.” Medical services rose “despite a decline in health insurance prices following the BLS’ incorporation of updated source data on insurance premiums.”

Logan's speech is now posted (link at the bottom - h/t @Fedwatchenjoyer), and a few other points stand out. 

She said this morning’s CPI “was higher than expected” and that “I am concerned that PCE inflation could rise when we receive those data for October in a couple of weeks.” 

She like Waller, though, isn't calling for a dramatic hiking cycle: “I currently estimate that the fed funds target range is at least 50 basis points—half a percentage point—below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target.” 

But she notes the real fed funds rate is just 78 basis points (the 3.88% fed funds rate less the roughly 3.1% inflation that households, businesses and markets expect), a quarter point below the lowest of eight model estimates of neutral, so “accommodative monetary policy is adding to inflationary pressures.”

And like the other Fed speakers since Thursday, she isn't moved by the market declines. Financial conditions “are currently providing a tailwind,” with credit spreads still “compressed by historical standards,” and the rise in 10-year yields is “more a message that investors believe monetary policy has work to do than an independent headwind for activity.”

On October’s skip, she said the volatile markets argued for moving “more gradually,” but “Skipping one meeting does not change the monetary policy destination,” and “the precise timing of each rate increase has little effect on the longer-term rates most borrowers pay.” After two more hikes, “it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments.”

And like Goolsbee yesterday, she pointed to services which came in elevated in October. “Prices for non-housing, non-transportation core services rose 3.2% over the 12 months ended in September,” eight tenths of a point above the pace consistent with the Fed’s target, and those prices “aren’t particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips.” 

But she downplayed her own bank’s inflation gauge. The Dallas Fed’s trimmed mean PCE was lower, at 2.3% over the 12 months through September, but she said her staff’s research finds “a change in the mix of price increases and decreases is causing the trimmed mean to drop too many increases right now,” which “likely makes the trimmed mean lower than the true inflation trend.”

Bloomberg Economics’ Anna Wong and Troy Durie say the report was not as bad as many are making out but change their call to a December hike: 

“October’s CPI report is the last one the FOMC will see before its Dec. 8-9 meeting – and it’s hot. For a Fed sounding the alarm on inflation, October’s CPI likely sealed the deal for a December rate hike.

@C_Barraud's Tuesday Brief has an interesting chart from JPMorgan Asset Management (via @dailychartbook): “History shows that large market moves are often followed by meaningful moves in the opposite direction.”

The data backs that up, with a catch (and scroll down further for what historically comes next):
▪️ Nine of the 10 historical moves on JPMorgan’s chart reversed the next day. Only March 24, 2020 didn’t.
▪️ But every one of them came with the S&P 500 already 16% to 46% below its high, consistent with typical big swings in both directions in bear markets: 17 of the 20 biggest up days since 1950 came 20% or more off the high, and none came within 10% of one.
▪️ In that regard, a big up day isn’t an all-clear. After the 11.6% gain on October 13, 2008, the index fell another 33% over the next year.

Last Thursday’s 4.4% drop started just 1.7% below the October 6 record, which is a different setup. Since 1950, a 4% one-day drop from within 5% of a record has happened only five other times:
▪️ September 1955 (Eisenhower’s heart attack), September 1986, October 1989 (Friday-the-13th mini-crash), October 1997 (the Asian crisis) and February 2018 (Volmageddon).
▪️ All five were higher three and six months later. Four of five were higher a year later, with 1989 the exception.
▪️ New record closes came 39 to 228 days later, with a median of 82.
▪️ The catch: 1989 and 2018, the two slowest to recover, both fell about 11% further along the way.

Also note this time the second big move came with a day's delay with Friday’s 0.3% gain before Monday’s 2.35% gain. The two days won back 59% of Thursday’s drop. That’s at the strong end of those five cases: 1955 won back 56% and 1997 65%, while 2018 won back only 29%. The S&P 500 is now 3.4% below its record.

The timing lesson holds: JPMorgan AM finds 7 of the 10 best days from 2005 to 2024 came within two weeks of one of the 10 worst. Selling into a shock usually means missing a rebound.

Also note it’s a small sample, so it's certainly not guaranteed.

October CPI preview: banks see core cooling, but probably not enough to stop a December hike.

Tuesday’s CPI is the last before the Fed’s December 8th–9th meeting. Bloomberg consensus is 0.3% for headline and 0.2% for core, after 0.65% and 0.33% in September (core’s most since April).

Five bank forecasts (headline / core / core PCE):

▪️ Goldman Sachs: 0.21% / 0.16% / 0.23%.

▪️ Morgan Stanley: 0.19% / 0.19% / 0.22%.

▪️ Bank of America: 0.17% / 0.22% / 0.23%.

▪️ Barclays: 0.24% / 0.22% / 0.21%.

▪️ JPMorgan: 0.25% / 0.23% / 0.23%.

All five core calls round to the 0.2% consensus, but four of five see headline below 0.3%. The core PCE readthrough is 0.21% to 0.23%, which BofA and JPMorgan say would push core PCE back up to 3.2% y/y.

Where they agree:
▪️ Shelter should cool. Owners’ equivalent rent jumped 0.35% in September, which Morgan Stanley calls “largely noise, amplified by unusual volatility in the Midwest,” and Goldman, BofA and JPMorgan all see 0.26% to 0.3%.

▪️ AI is showing up in goods prices. BofA says IT commodities added roughly 90bp to core goods’ 2.4% annualized three-month pace, and Morgan Stanley cites “AI-related price pressures.”

▪️A December hike is likely. BofA says its forecast “would effectively lock in another 25bp hike,” and that it would take “an indisputably soft 0.1% m/m print” to change the Fed’s mind. Barclays sees October as “a pause, rather than a reversal."  JPM says "a very
soft number could raise questions about a hike next month, but that is not our expectation," and a third straight 0.3% would challenge market pricing for only one more hike next year. Morgan Stanley expects hikes in December and March. 

Where they disagree:
▪️ Health insurance gets its semiannual source-data update. Goldman and JPMorgan see about −2.5%, BofA −0.9%, while Barclays expects a firmer run-rate.

▪️ Used cars: Goldman sees −1.5% based on auction prices, BofA flat and JPMorgan +0.4%.

▪️ Energy: BofA sees −0.38%, while Goldman and JPMorgan see +0.5%.

An under-the-radar story with a lot riding on it flagged in @C_Barraud’s Morning Brief: Israeli President Herzog has given Gadi Eisenkot the first shot at forming a government. That puts Netanyahu’s record tenure closer to its end than at any point in years.

Where things stand after the Oct. 27 vote:

▪️ Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats and Eisenkot’s 48. The Arab-led parties surged to 19 (+9). Nobody got the 61 needed for a majority.
▪️ But Eisenkot got 67 recommendations, including both Arab-led lists, vs. 46 for Netanyahu. That is why he got the mandate even though Likud is still the largest party at 27 seats.
▪️ He has 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension, to put a coalition together.

This is being treated by many as a binary outcome. If Eisenkot succeeds, Netanyahu and his religious-nationalist partners go to the opposition. That could come through a “national emergency government” or a minority government kept alive by outside Arab or ultra-Orthodox support. 

If Eisenkot fails, the mandate likely goes back to Netanyahu. If Netanyahu can’t form a government either, Israel heads to new elections within 90 days, probably in early spring, with Netanyahu staying on as caretaker.

That’s where Netanyahu likely wins even in a stalemate. First, he remains in power throughout the process.  Second, Eisenkot’s camp was carried by two turnout surges that will be hard to repeat:

▪️ Record Arab turnout, with estimates above 77% vs. roughly 53% last time.
▪️ Tens of thousands of expat Israelis flying home to vote, since Israel has no absentee voting for ordinary citizens.

A rerun a few months from now looks set up to tilt back toward Netanyahu.

The path for Eisenkot is narrow. He has set conditions aimed at the Arab parties, including recognizing Israel as a Jewish state and Hamas as a terrorist group. The ultra-Orthodox parties hold 13 seats and want draft exemptions, while equal military service was central to his campaign. Then there’s the Iran wildcard: if the US renews strikes, the pressure shifts toward a unity government with Netanyahu.

Tel Aviv stocks rallied about 2% in the last session before the vote, and the shekel hit a five-week high as investors priced in a change of government. Both reversed when the deadlock became clear. The shekel fell 2.2% to around 3.12/$, its weakest close in more than six months, and the TA-125 dropped 2.5%. JPMorgan had estimated the election alone could move the shekel by as much as 3%. The next six weeks decide which way that risk premium goes.
